item.title: JS Speaker to hold press conference at 5pm following President’s resignation
item.description:
Jatiya Sangsad (national parliament) Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad has called an emergency press conference, which is scheduled to take place at 5:00 pm today, Friday.

According to a press release issued by the Assistant Director of the Public Relations Wing of the Jatiya Sangsad Secretariat, the briefing will be held in the Parliament Oath Room following the Speaker’s acceptance of the President's letter of resignation.

The Speaker returned to Dhaka from Bangkok on Friday afternoon. He had travelled to the Thailand capital on 19 July for a medical check-up.

Speaking to newspersons at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport at around 12:15 pm, Hafiz Uddin Ahmad said he had no knowledge of the President's resignation.

Responding to a question, he said, “I do not know what the President will or will not do. He is the First Citizen of the country.”

Asked further about the possibility of the President stepping down, the Speaker said, “I was outside the country. Therefore, I have no knowledge of whether anyone intends to resign. I may know more now. If the President resigns, the resignation will be submitted to the Speaker. The Jatiya Sangsad will elect a new President within 90 days. That is the parliamentary convention.”

When asked why he had cut short his visit to Bangkok, the Speaker replied, “I had some personal matters to attend to in Dhaka. As my medical check-up was completed yesterday, I decided to return home.”

Responding to questions about assuming presidential responsibilities in case of the resignation, the Speaker said, “This is written in the Constitution of Bangladesh. When the President resigns, the Speaker serves as Acting President. The Jatiya Sangsad elects the President, and that election must be held within three months. That is the constitutional position.”

Hafiz Uddin Ahmad had travelled from Dhaka to Bangkok on 19 July for medical treatment. His return two days earlier than scheduled has further fuelled speculation over the possible resignation of President Mohammed Shahabuddin, as under the Constitution the President submits a resignation letter to the Speaker, who then assumes the role of Acting President until a new Head of State is elected.

For several days, there has been widespread speculation that President Mohammed Shahabuddin may resign.

item.title: School of Noize: Khulna University alumni reconnect through an original music legacy
item.description:
Khulna University has produced generations of musicians, but many never shared the same stage or rehearsal room. Over time, bands disappeared, songs remained unreleased, and stories stayed within small circles. School of Noize, presented by KUsician Collaboration, was created to bring part of that scattered history back into one frame.

The project is an original multi-solo instrumental video, not a cover. It grew from an alumni-led idea to reconnect Khulna University musicians across generations through one original piece. Instead of choosing a cover, the collaboration was built around an original backing theme created within the same alumni music circle, later expanded by participants through guitars, bass, drums, keys, indigenous instruments, and other sounds.

The collaboration brought together 34 amateur and semi-professional musicians from Batch ’96 to ’26, representing around 14 disciplines and 19 campus bands, with contributors in Bangladesh and abroad reports a press release. For several senior participants, it became their first proper recording experience; for younger musicians, it opened a space to learn from the writing, recording, tone-shaping, and collaboration process.

The collaboration matters because of its context: Khulna University’s music culture grew without ready-made rehearsal spaces, studios, formal facilities, or easy access to major networks. For many outside Dhaka, it was sustained by borrowed instruments, improvised spaces, limited equipment, academic pressure, institutional resistance, and the sheer will to keep playing.

The title was chosen through voting and echoes Noise Factory, the Khulna University rock and metal forum founded in 2009 and banned in 2023. Remembered as a pioneering university-based band music forum, a long-running campus gig platform, and a regional force in southern Bangladesh’s rock and metal culture, Noise Factory drew its name from a phrase shared by the father of one of its founding members: “music is an expensive noise.”

That “noise” was often misunderstood. One Director of Student Affairs reportedly labelled the name “vulgar,” while another had earlier described Eclipse, one of Khulna University’s earliest bands, as “unsocial music.” Some of those involved allege that Noise Factory’s activities were unjustly stopped by the university authorities in 2023.

With Noise Factory no longer active, School of Noize is both a bittersweet farewell to that era and possibly among the first alumni-based original multi-solo instrumental collaborations of its kind in Bangladesh. Above all, it is a thank-you note to Khulna University — and a reminder to record, create, document, and pass the noise forward.

item.title: President Shahabuddin resigns, Speaker to assume presidential duties
item.description:
President Mohammed Shahabuddin has resigned from office. Following the acceptance of his resignation letter, Speaker of the Jatiya Sangsad (national parliament) Hafiz Uddin Ahmad has called a press conference, which will be held at 5:00 pm at the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban.

With the office of the President now vacant, the Speaker will assume the duties of Acting President, in accordance with the Constitution, until a new President takes office.

Under Article 50(3) of the Constitution of Bangladesh, the President may resign by submitting a signed letter addressed to the Speaker.

Article 54 provides that, if the office of the President becomes vacant, or if the President is unable to discharge the functions of the office due to absence, illness or any other reason, the Speaker shall perform the functions of the President until a new President is elected and assumes office.

Under Article 123(2) of the Constitution, if the office of the President falls vacant due to death, resignation or removal, a new President must be elected within 90 days. Under Article 48(1), the President is elected by a vote of the members of parliament.

The ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) has a two-third majority in parliament, making its nominee the overwhelming favourite to become the next President.

Senior BNP leaders have been holding discussions over the past several days on who should be nominated as Mohammed Shahabuddin’s successor.

Earlier today, Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad returned to Dhaka from Bangkok, where he had travelled on 19 July for medical treatment.

Although he had originally been scheduled to return on Sunday, he cut short his visit and arrived in Bangladesh two days ahead of schedule.

Speaking to journalists at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport at around 12:15 pm, before the resignation was announced, the Speaker said he had no knowledge of any plan by the President to step down.

Noting that he had been abroad, Hafiz Uddin Ahmad stated that if the President were to resign, the resignation letter would be submitted to the Speaker. In that case, the Speaker would assume the functions of Acting President under the Constitution, while the Jatiya Sangsad would elect a new President within 90 days.

Speculation over President Mohammed Shahabuddin’s possible resignation had intensified in political circles over the past several days.

On Thursday, informed sources indicated that he had become mentally prepared to step down. One source familiar with the matter also claimed that, during a meeting with senior officials at Bangabhaban, the President had spoken of making preparations for his departure from office.

Mohammed Shahabuddin assumed office as Bangladesh's 22nd President on 24 April 2023, during the tenure of the Awami League government, for a constitutional term of five years. His term had been due to expire in April 2028, but he resigned nearly two years before completing his tenure.

Following the fall of the Sheikh Hasina government during the July 2024 mass uprising, Mohammed Shahabuddin's continuation in office became the subject of sustained political debate.

The discussion intensified after the BNP returned to power following the 13th Jatiya Sangsad election. His resignation has now brought about a change at the country's highest constitutional office.

item.title: President Mohammed Shahabuddin resigns
item.description:
President Mohammed Shahabuddin resigned on Friday by submitting his resignation letter to Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad, triggering the constitutional process for an interim presidency.
In his resignation letter, Shahabuddin said he was no longer physically and mentally capable of carrying out the responsibilities of the constitutional office due to multiple health complications.
He wrote: “I am seriously ill. I am suffering from heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes and kidney complications. I have undergone bypass surgery on my heart. Recently, a medical examination diagnosed me with a disease called Autonomic Neuropathy. Because of this disease, I occasionally lose consciousness for brief periods. Due to the combined effects of these illnesses and the resulting physical and mental incapacity, it is no longer possible for me to discharge the responsibilities of such an important constitutional office as the President. I require long-term medical treatment.
In these circumstances, in accordance with the provisions of Article 50(3) of the Constitution, I hereby resign from the office of the President.”
National Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad called an emergency press briefing at 5pm on Friday.
Under Article 54 of the Constitution, the speaker will perform the duties of the president until a new president takes office following the vacancy in the office.
Article 54 states that if the office of the president becomes vacant, or if the president is unable to perform the duties of the office because of absence, illness, or any other reason, the speaker shall perform the duties of the president until a new president is elected.
Article 123(2) of the Constitution states: “If the office of the president becomes vacant due to death, resignation or removal, a new president must be elected within the next 90 days.”
Mohammed Shahabuddin served as a commissioner of the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) from 2011 to 2016 before becoming Bangladesh’s 22nd president on April 24, 2023, during the Awami League government, for a 5-year term.
He was due to remain in office until April 2028 but resigned nearly 2 years before completing his tenure.
Following the political changeover on August 5, 2024, several political parties, including the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement, demanded his removal. The interim government did not remove him, citing constitutional reasons, and the issue later subsided.
After the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) formed the government following its victory in the National Parliament election on February 12, discussions over replacing the president resurfaced. BNP leaders said in March that the matter had not been discussed within the party because the president still had time remaining in his tenure. News of Shahabuddin's resignation emerged 4 months later.

Thousands flee wildfires in France, Spain
item.description:
Luggage-laden residents and tourists fled a French peninsula by boat and the smell of smoke drifted into parts of Madrid on Friday as wildfires swept France and Spain, triggering states of emergencies and calls for EU help.
In France, fires scorching through dense pine forests near the prized wine region of Bordeaux forced hundreds to flee the upscale Cap Ferret peninsula in the middle of the summer holiday season, as the blaze devoured an area nearly twice the size of Manhattan.
Several blazes were also raging out of control less than 100 kilometers from Madrid, with some residents of the Spanish capital waking up to the smell of smoke.
Two fires west of the city were on the verge of merging and “becoming a single blaze advancing towards Navas del Rey,” a town some 50 kilometers from Madrid’s outskirts, said Francisco Martin, a senior local official.
Thick acrid smoke billowed into the sky as a wall of fire crept along parched earth, according to aerial images by Spanish authorities.
Fanned by wind and scorching temperatures topping 40°C in some areas, the blazes have killed three firefighters and forced the evacuation of some 50,000 people in the two countries.
“The smoke was incredibly thick. You couldn’t breathe,” Jose Cobos, who fled his home some 50 kilometers southwest of Madrid with his wife and three dogs, told Antena 3 television as he waited anxiously to learn if his house was still standing.
French authorities have ordered thousands of tourists on the southwestern Atlantic coast out of campsites and holiday homes, as firefighters backed by water-bombing planes raced to control the blazes.
More than 40,000 people have been evacuated in the region so far.
Both France and Spain have appealed to the European Union for help, with Madrid requesting four specialized planes on Friday, a day after Paris asked Brussels for more resources.
The European Union said it was deploying four planes to Spain and three to France to help fight the blazes.
“We are living through a dramatic situation, not only in various Spanish provinces but also in regions of neighboring countries,” Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez wrote on X, saying the government “has deployed all available resources.”
In Spain, the government declared a state of emergency in the Madrid region, where more than 10,000 people have been evacuated in recent days, including more than 400 elderly and people with disabilities whisked away from several care homes.
“Meteorological conditions, fundamentally the wind, will complicate firefighting operations this Friday,” the Madrid regional government said in a post on X.
France’s southeast was also being hard hit, with Interior Minister Laurent Nunez saying that 32 fires of various intensity were raging across the country.
“We have passed the threshold of 50,000 hectares that have burnt since January 1 of this year,” an area nearly five times the size of Paris, said Nunez, adding that the figure was nearly three times that of last year.
One firefighter has died after falling ill while battling the flames in Sicily, the interior minister said.
Two firefighters died on Tuesday tackling another blaze near Bordeaux airport.
The total area of land burnt so far this year in EU countries is the second largest on record, according to satellite data from the European Forest Fire Information System (Effis).
The blazes are breaking out faster because of the current European drought, made more severe by human-caused climate change, scientists from the World Weather Attribution group said in a study published this week.
Spanish civil protection chief Virginia Barcones warned on Spanish radio that some fires have become so intense that, despite the deployment of aircraft and ground crews, firefighters stand “no chance.”

item.title: India’s youth-led ‘Cockroach’ movement holds new round of talks with govt
item.description:
Leaders of India’s youth-led “Cockroach” movement held a second round of talks with government officials on Friday, after Prime Minister Narendra Modi pledged legal reforms and swift punishment for those involved in exam paper leaks.
The Indian capital has been rocked by demonstrations led by the social media-driven Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) this week, which has demanded an overhaul of the education system and the resignation of the education minister after repeated testing scandals.
In one of the biggest challenges to Hindu-nationalist Modi’s administration since his 2024 re-election for a third term, thousands have been protesting calling for reform -- with Monday’s marches turning into violent clashes with police.
At the Jantar Mantar protest site, student Sushmita, 20 said she felt the government dragged its feet on the issue for too long.
“Why did it take the government this long to announce the steps?” she told AFP.
“I don’t know how Modi and this government can come back to us for support during the next elections.”
The protest has since evolved to include concerns over unemployment, opportunities for young people and what critics have called Modi’s increasingly authoritarian style of governance.
“We hope that the government comes with an open mind and it will listen to the people of this country who have been out on the roads for so long,” a spokesperson from the youth-led movement Saurav Das told reporters ahead of Friday’s meeting with senior ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh.
“We will explain our demands to them in detail. And we hope that the government will listen to us,” Das said.
India’s opposition parties backed the protest and disrupted proceedings in the lower house of parliament Friday, urging Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to step down before any debate on proposed reforms takes place.
“You (opposition parties) have been asking for a debate since the start and the government is ready. Don’t put any conditions,” Kiren Rijiju from Modi’s ruling Bhartiya Janata Party (BJP) said.
“I don’t understand why we can’t have a good and healthy discussion on this issue.”
In a late-night social media post, Modi said his cabinet would discuss measures on Friday to speed up court proceedings against those involved in examination leaks. His post did not mention Pradhan’s resignation.
After “incorporating the suggestions of my cabinet colleagues,” a draft legislation would be given “its final shape,” he said.
“We will make every effort to have the bill introduced and passed by the House at the earliest,” Modi added.
The prime minister’s intervention followed mounting pressure from protesters and civil rights groups and a first round of talks with Nadda on Monday.
Prominent activist Sonam Wangchuk, who ended a 26-day hunger strike in support of the movement late Thursday, said the government had assured him that no action would be taken against peaceful demonstrators.
“They also assured us that parliament would hold a full debate on the issue and on improving accountability in the education and examination system,” he said on social media.
Protests escalated on Monday when police fired tear gas and used batons against tens of thousands of demonstrators in New Delhi, the capital’s largest street rally in five years.
Founder of the social media movement Abhijeet Dipke welcomed Wangchuk’s decision to end his hunger strike but said the movement would continue until their demands are met.
“By putting your own life on the line, you awakened the conscience of an entire nation,” Dipke, 30, said in a social media post, referring to Wangchuk.

item.title: EU accuses TikTok of exposing children to risks online
item.description:
The European Union on Friday accused TikTok of failing to protect children since their account settings expose them to risks like cyberbullying and predatory behavior -- putting the company at risk of a large fine.
The EU said minors’ accounts should only be visible to those they have given permission. Children aged 13 and over can use TikTok.
“A high level of protection should not be an opt-in; it should be the default,” EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
TikTok insisted it was committed to protecting minors online.
The EU has intensified its efforts to protect minors with new rules expected later this year that will ban children under the age of 13 using social media.
Brussels began its probe into Chinese-owned TikTok in 2024 under the Digital Services Act (DSA) -- a content law and major weapon in the EU’s boosted legal armory that it has deployed to rein in Big Tech in recent years.
Under the DSA, children’s account settings have, by default, the strongest safety and security protections.
“TikTok’s account settings fail to meet this standard, as they expose minors’ accounts and content too widely,” the EU said in its preliminary view.
The EU found during the investigation that minors can make their account public, meaning anyone with or without a TikTok account can see their content.
Even when children choose to make their accounts private, they can be “easily found” through other users’ “following” and “followers” lists.
“TikTok’s settings continue to expose them to risks -– including unwanted contact, cyberbullying, or predatory behavior,” the EU warned.
Brussels told TikTok to adjust the default settings for minors’ “public” accounts, making them only visible to users whom the child has accepted.
A TikTok spokesperson said teen accounts have more than 50 preset privacy and safety features and stressed under-18 accounts were private by default.
“We will review these preliminary findings as we continue to engage constructively” with the EU, the spokesperson added.
If the EU’s views on TikTok are confirmed, the EU can slap a fine of up to six percent of the company’s total worldwide annual turnover.
The EU already took an unprecedented step in February against TikTok when it told the platform to change its addictive design or face heavy fines.
Meta has faced similar scrutiny after Brussels told the tech titan two weeks ago to change its addictive design features such as infinite scrolling.
The mood in Europe is turning against letting younger children access social media and other digital platforms. France this week became the first EU nation to block social media for under-15s.
Experts tasked by EU chief Ursula von der Leyen recommended earlier this month that the 27-country bloc should prohibit children under the age of 13 from having their own social media accounts.
Von der Leyen is due to announce in September what the EU’s approach will be but has indicated that she backed the experts’ recommendations.
The EU is also preparing to rollout an age verification app across the bloc to make sure platforms check the ages of users before accessing platforms.

item.title: Speaker Hafiz Uddin takes charge as Acting President
item.description:
Speaker of the Jatiya Sangsad Hafiz Uddin Ahmad, Bir Bikram, has assumed the responsibilities of the Acting President in accordance with the Constitution after accepting the resignation of Mohammed Shahabuddin.

“Under Article 50(3) of the Constitution, President Mohammed Shahabuddin submitted his signed letter of resignation to the Speaker at 5:01pm on Friday. After accepting the resignation, I have assumed the responsibilities of the President in accordance with Article 54 of the Constitution”, the speaker disclosed it at a press conference held at the oath room of the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban on Friday afternoon.

He said Mohammed Shahabuddin, in his resignation letter, stated that he was suffering from serious health complications, including heart disease, hypertension, diabetes and kidney-related ailments.

Mohammed Shahabuddin had previously undergone coronary bypass surgery, while recent medical examinations diagnosed him with autonomic neuropathy, a condition that occasionally causes him to lose consciousness, the speaker said.

“Due to these physical complications and resulting mental incapacity, it has become impossible for him (Mohammed Shahabuddin) to discharge his constitutional responsibilities as President.

He has, therefore, resigned as he requires long-term medical treatment,” Hafiz Uddin Ahmad said, referring to the contents of the resignation letter.

He said that under the Constitution, when a Speaker takes oath, it also includes the oath required to discharge the responsibilities of the Acting President whenever necessary.

He added that if the office of the Speaker falls vacant, the Deputy Speaker will perform the duties of the Speaker in accordance with the constitutional provisions.

Referring to public discussions over the President’s resignation, the Speaker said it was now clear that the resignation was solely due to health reasons.

He wished Mohammed Shahabuddin a speedy recovery and good health.

Replying to questions from journalists, the Speaker said a President could fall ill and the written resignation itself clearly explained the medical reasons behind the decision.

“In such a case, no additional medical certificate is required,” he said, expressing hope that the resignation would remove all confusion, speculation and uncertainty surrounding the issue.

He further said the office of the President never remains vacant under the Constitution.

“As the Speaker of the Jatiya Sangsad, I accepted the resignation and have accordingly begun discharging the responsibilities of the President,” he added.

Jatiya Sangsad Chief Whip Md Nurul Islam, Deputy Speaker Barrister Kayser Kamal and senior officials of the Jatiya Sangsad Secretariat were present at the press conference.

item.title: ‘Although elected during mafia regime, he supported people’s govt’
item.description:
While announcing the resignation of President Mohammed Shahabuddin, Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad also offered a personal assessment of the outgoing Head of State.

Assuming the responsibilities of Acting President under the Constitution, Hafiz Uddin Ahmad said, “I think, although he (Mohammed Shahabuddin) was elected during the mafia regime, he consistently expressed his support for, and respect towards, the government elected by the people’s vote. I wish him well.”

The Speaker returned to Bangladesh on Friday afternoon after cutting short an overseas visit amid speculation over the President’s possible resignation.

Addressing a press conference at Parliament at 5:30 pm today, he announced that President Shahabuddin had resigned on health grounds and that the resignation letter had been submitted to him earlier in the day.

He added that, in accordance with the Constitution, he had assumed the duties of Acting President.

Mohammed Shahabuddin was elected unopposed as President on 24 April 2023 as the nominee of the Awami League government. Although demands for his removal emerged after the fall of the Awami League government during the 2024 student-led mass uprising, he remained in office.

President Shahabuddin resigns, Speaker to assume presidential duties

He resigned nearly two years before the expiry of his five-year term, around five months after the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) formed the government following the 13th general election in February.

The Speaker said the resignation letter cited ill health as the reason for stepping down. Referring to Article 50(3) of the Constitution, he said the President submitted his signed resignation letter to the Speaker at 5:01 pm, together with a written explanation stating that serious health problems had left him unable to carry out the constitutional responsibilities of the office.

Hafiz Uddin Ahmad outlined the medical conditions listed by the President, saying that he suffers from heart disease, hypertension, diabetes and kidney-related complications. He had previously undergone coronary artery bypass surgery, and recent medical examinations diagnosed him with autonomic neuropathy, a condition that causes intermittent episodes of loss of consciousness.

According to the Speaker, the cumulative effect of these illnesses, together with the resulting physical and mental incapacity, had made it impossible for the President to continue discharging the duties of such a high constitutional office.

He said the President had decided to resign because he required long-term medical treatment.

The Speaker also confirmed that the resignation letter had been formally accepted, preserved in the records of the Jatiya Sangsad Secretariat, and that the necessary administrative procedures had been initiated.

Reasons cited for President Shahabuddin’s resignation

Referring to Article 54 of the Constitution, Hafiz Uddin Ahmad announced that, with the presidency now vacant, he had assumed the functions of Acting President.

He further explained that, when he took the oath of office as Speaker, he had simultaneously taken the constitutional oath enabling him to perform the functions of the President if required. Likewise, should the office of the Speaker become vacant, the Deputy Speaker would assume those responsibilities in accordance with the Constitution.

The Speaker kept the press conference brief, taking only two questions despite numerous requests from journalists.

Responding to a question about the speculation surrounding the President’s resignation, he said, “After returning to Bangladesh this afternoon, I heard many different rumours. It is now clear that he resigned because of physical incapacity. I wish him good health and a speedy recovery.”

It was in response to that question that Hafiz Uddin Ahmad offered his assessment of Mohammed Shahabuddin. Notably, it was President Shahabuddin himself who had administered the Speaker’s oath of office on 12 March this year.

Asked whether medical certification was required to substantiate the President’s resignation, the Speaker replied, “The resignation of the President is a serious constitutional matter and has important implications for the country.”

“The President is a human being and may become ill. He has disclosed the names of his illnesses in writing and stated that he occasionally loses consciousness. Under these circumstances, there is no need for a physician’s certificate when he himself has formally declared his medical condition,” he added.

Hafiz Uddin Ahmad also said there should be no room for uncertainty over the President’s resignation.

“We hope this resignation has removed all ambiguity. There should be no disorder, misunderstanding or confusion arising from this matter. Presidents have resigned in Bangladesh before for various reasons. The President is a respected constitutional office-holder and has every right to resign. The office never remains vacant. As Speaker of the Jatiya Sangsad, I have accepted the resignation letter. That is the constitutional reality. I hope all confusion will now come to an end,” he stated.

With the presidency now vacant following the resignation of President Mohammed Shahabuddin on Friday, political attention has turned to who will become Bangladesh's 23rd president.
Shahabuddin submitted his signed resignation letter to Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmed on Friday afternoon. Under the Constitution, the resignation took effect immediately upon its submission to the speaker.
Article 123 of the Constitution stipulates that if the office of the president becomes vacant, Parliament must elect a new president within 90 days through a vote of Members of Parliament (MPs). Until then, the speaker will continue to discharge the duties of acting president.
Under the Constitution, the President is elected by MPs. As the ruling alliance holds a parliamentary majority, its nominated candidate is expected to secure the presidency.
According to multiple BNP sources, BNP Secretary General and Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir is the frontrunner in discussions to become the country's next president. The sources said that if the party makes a final decision in his favor, he is expected to resign from both his cabinet position and party post before assuming the constitutional office.
Other names under consideration include BNP Standing Committee members Dr Khandaker Mosharraf Hossain and Dr Abdul Moyeen Khan. Party insiders said several other senior leaders are also being discussed informally.
The sources said the final decision is expected to be based on political acceptability, the ability to discharge constitutional responsibilities, seniority within the party, and the current political landscape.
Neither the government nor the BNP leadership has officially commented on the matter. Senior leaders from both sides said the final decision on the next president will be made by Prime Minister and BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman. They said an official announcement would come after consultations at the highest levels of the party and government and a review of the relevant political and constitutional considerations.
Several BNP policymakers said the next president would likely have to navigate political challenges surrounding the next parliamentary election. They added that experience in working with the government, opposition parties, and state institutions, as well as broad political acceptability, would be important considerations in selecting the country's next head of state.
A state minister said: "Following the President's resignation, the Speaker will perform the duties of Acting President. Our prime minister will decide who the next President will be. We believe a senior party leader is likely to be nominated."
The BNP secured a majority in the 13th parliamentary election held on February 12 and formed the government on February 17. On the same day, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman announced his cabinet, while the first session of the 13th National Parliament began on March 12.
Mohammed Shahabuddin was elected unopposed as president in 2023 with the nomination of the Awami League. His 5-year term was originally scheduled to expire in April 2028.

item.title: Life after Bangabhaban: What former presidents get
item.description:
Former presidents of Bangladesh who resign after serving at least 6 months or complete a full term are entitled to a lifetime pension and other government benefits under the President's Pension, Gratuity and Other Benefits Act, 2016.
The law, enacted by Parliament in 2016, repealed the President's Pension Ordinance issued in 1979.
Section 3 of the law provides that a president who resigns after serving at least 6 months or completes a full term is entitled to a lifetime pension.
The monthly pension is set at 75% of the last basic monthly salary received while serving as president. With the president's current basic salary fixed at Tk 120,000, an eligible former president receives a monthly pension of Tk 90,000.
A former president may choose a one-time gratuity instead of the monthly pension.
The gratuity is calculated by multiplying 1 year's pension by the number of years served as president.
If a former president dies while receiving the pension, the spouse is entitled to a lifetime family allowance equal to two-thirds of the pension payable to the former president.
Under Section 5 of the law, former presidents are entitled to several government facilities in addition to the pension.
These include 1 personal assistant and 1 attendant for official and personal work.
Former presidents are also entitled to lifetime government medical facilities equivalent to those provided to a serving cabinet minister.
They are provided with a residential telephone connection at government expense and are entitled to stay free of charge at government circuit houses or rest houses while traveling within the country.
For international travel, they are entitled to use a government-issued diplomatic passport.
Section 6 of the law sets out conditions under which a former president is not eligible for these benefits.
A president removed from office through impeachment under Article 52 of the Constitution is not entitled to receive any benefit under the law.
The law also disqualifies any person declared by the higher judiciary to have seized power through unconstitutional means, as well as any former president convicted by a court of an offense involving moral turpitude.

item.title: Acting President Hafiz Uddin Ahmad assumes office, receives floral greetings
item.description:
Acting President and National Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad, Bir Bikram, received a floral reception after assuming the responsibilities of the president on Friday afternoon.
Among those who greeted the acting president with floral bouquets were National Parliament Deputy Speaker Barrister Kayser Kamal, Chief Whip Md Nurul Islam, Attorney General Barrister Ruhul Quddus Kajal, and Bangladesh National Parliament Secretariat Secretary Barrister Md Golam Sorwar Bhuiyan, according to a press release issued by the National Parliament Secretariat.
Earlier on Friday, President Mohammed Sahabuddin submitted his resignation letter to the speaker of the National Parliament in accordance with Article 50(3) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the release said.
Following the resignation, Hafiz Uddin Ahmad, Bir Bikram, assumed the responsibilities of the president under Article 54 of the Constitution, becoming the acting president of the People's Republic of Bangladesh until further constitutional arrangements are made.

item.title: Speaker confirms acceptance of President's resignation
item.description:
Speaker of the National Parliament Hafiz Uddin Ahmed on Friday confirmed that he had accepted President Mohammed Shahabuddin's letter of resignation.
President's Military Secretary Major General ASM Bahauddin delivered the signed resignation letter to the office of Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmed at the National Parliament at around 4:00pm on Friday.
"Under Article 50(3) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, President Mohammed Shahabuddin submitted his signed letter of resignation to me at 5:01pm on July 24. In accordance with Article 54 of the Constitution, I have assumed the responsibilities of the President. I have accepted the resignation letter and instructed the National Parliament Secretariat to place it on official record and undertake the necessary administrative procedures," Hafiz Uddin Ahmed said at a press briefing at 5:00pm.
Amid mounting speculation over the President's resignation, the Speaker had earlier cut short a personal visit to Thailand and returned to Bangladesh.
Explaining the reason for the president's resignation, the Speaker said it was only natural that the public would want to know why he had stepped down.
Reading from the president's written resignation letter, the Speaker said he had cited serious health complications as the reason for leaving office.
"He has been suffering from heart disease, hypertension, diabetes and kidney-related complications, and has previously undergone coronary bypass surgery," the Speaker said.
He added that the president had recently been diagnosed with autonomic neuropathy, a condition that causes intermittent loss of consciousness.
"The progression of these illnesses, coupled with his physical and mental incapacity, has made it impossible for him to discharge the responsibilities of the presidency, a high constitutional office. He requires long-term medical treatment. For these health reasons, he has resigned, and as Speaker of the National Parliament, I have accepted his resignation letter," the Speaker said.
Confirming the constitutional transition, the Speaker said he had already taken the oath as Acting President on the day he was sworn in as Speaker.
"When I took the oath as Speaker, I also took the oath as Acting President. The Constitution provides for this. The office of the President never remains vacant," he said.
Referring to the ongoing public debate surrounding the president's resignation, the Speaker said speculation had been rife across the country but stressed that the decision was made solely on health grounds.
"There has been a great deal of discussion across Bangladesh today. I heard many of these conversations as soon as I arrived on Friday afternoon. But the fact is that he resigned because of physical incapacity," the Speaker said.
Concluding the briefing, the Speaker wished the president a speedy recovery and acknowledged his support for the current administration.
"I wish him good health and a full recovery. Although he was elected during the tenure of the previous government, which has been described as a fascist regime, I believe he has consistently shown respect for and support toward the present government, which was elected by the people. I wish him all the best," the Speaker said.

item.title: Dengue cases surge sharply in Chittagong
item.description:
Dengue infections have risen sharply in Chittagong with the onset of the monsoon, as the number of cases recorded in the first 23 days of July has already exceeded the total reported during the previous six months.
According to the Chittagong Civil Surgeon’s Office, 356 people were hospitalized with dengue between July 1 and July 23, compared with 298 cases recorded from January through June. Overall, 654 dengue patients have been admitted to hospitals in the district between January 1 and July 23, while two people have died from the disease.
Health officials attributed the sharp increase to continuous rainfall, stagnant water, and the rapid breeding of Aedes mosquitoes, warning that infections could rise further unless mosquito control measures are strengthened and public awareness improves.
Data show that July has become the worst month of the year so far, with 356 infections recorded in just 23 days, compared with 122 in June, 37 in May, 29 in April, 20 in March, 22 in February, and 68 in January. Of the total patients, 260 are residents of Chittagong city, 262 are from the district’s upazilas, and 132 are from other districts under the division, while 376 are men, 165 are women, and 113 are children.
A recent survey by Chittagong Divisional Health Department found Aedes mosquitoes in every ward of the city and identified eight wards as the most vulnerable to dengue transmission: North Kattali (Ward 10), Pahartali (Ward 3), Alkaran (Ward 2), West Bakalia (Ward 17), South Bakalia (Ward 19), South Halishahar (Ward 39), Patharghata (Ward 34), and Andarkilla (Ward 32).
The survey showed that 70–80% of the mosquitoes collected were Aedes aegypti, the primary carrier of the dengue virus, while the remaining 20–30% were Aedes albopictus. Among the district’s 15 upazilas, Sitakunda reported the highest number of infections with 64 cases, followed by Lohagara and Raozan with 23 each, Patiya and Mirsharai with 18 each, Banshkhali with 16, Satkania with 15, Anwara with 13, Rangunia with 11, Hathazari with 8, Chandanaish with 7, Sandwip with 6, Fatikchhari with 4, and Boalkhali with 2 cases.
Chittagong Civil Surgeon Dr. Jahangir Alam said dengue is a mosquito-borne disease and stressed that eliminating mosquito breeding sites remains the most effective way to curb transmission. He said all government hospitals have been equipped with the necessary medicines and treatment facilities, while the Health Department has completed preparations to cope with a possible increase in patients.
City Corporation officials said mosquito control operations have been intensified across all 41 wards, with a trained 60-member team deployed to spray insecticides in hotspot areas and 205 spray workers conducting regular larvicide operations, while sufficient insecticide stocks have been secured for the next six months.

item.title: PM invites Qatari investment through letter to amir
item.description:

Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman handed over the letter to Qatar's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Sultan bin Saad Al-Muraikhi during a bilateral meeting in Manila on Friday, said a foreign ministry's press release here.
The meeting was held on the sidelines of the 50th anniversary commemoration of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia (TAC).

item.title: Thailand likely to employ 10,000 Bangladeshis
item.description:
Bangladesh and Thailand have discussed the prospect of employment for around 10,000 Bangladeshi workers in Thailand following completion of necessary procedures, alongside expanding bilateral cooperation in trade, investment and tourism.
The issue was discussed during a bilateral meeting between Prime Minister's Foreign Affairs Adviser Humaiun Kobir and Thai Deputy Foreign Minister Vijavat Isarabhakdi in Bangkok on Friday morning, according to a press release received here on Friday.
Humaiun held the meeting during a stopover in the Thai capital following his official visit to Manila, the Philippines.
During the talks, the two sides reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening the longstanding friendly relations between Bangladesh and Thailand and expanding cooperation in the areas of mutual interest.
They reviewed the overall state of bilateral relations and discussed ways to enhance cooperation in trade and investment, labour mobility, tourism and people-to-people contacts.
The two sides particularly exchanged views on the prospect of opening employment opportunities for around 10,000 Bangladeshi workers in Thailand once the necessary procedures are completed.
The Foreign Affairs adviser also sought Thailand's continued support for Bangladesh's inclusion as an Asean Sectoral Dialogue Partner.
In response, the Thai deputy foreign minister assured that Thailand would continue its constructive engagement on the matter.
Bangladesh has been seeking Asean Sectoral Dialogue Partner status as part of its broader efforts to deepen institutional engagement with the Southeast Asian regional bloc and strengthen economic and strategic ties with its member states.
During the meeting, Humaiun, on behalf of the prime minister of Bangladesh, also invited the Thai prime minister to visit Bangladesh at a mutually convenient time.

item.title: Info minister: All religious communities enjoy equal rights in Bangladesh
item.description:
Information and Broadcasting Minister Zahir Uddin Swapon has said citizens of all religious faiths in Bangladesh enjoy equal rights, emphasizing that the country's constitution leaves no scope for discrimination or division based on religion.
"Sanatan believers enjoy the exact same rights as Muslims, Christians, and Buddhists in this country. Our constitution does not divide people on the basis of religion. Those who attempt to create division in the name of religion or politics are enemies of the nation, enemies of religion, and enemies of the Almighty," he said.
The minister made the remarks while addressing as the chief guest at a discussion organized on the occasion of Sri Sri Jagannathdev's Ulto Rath Yatra at the Dhakeshwari National Temple in the capital on Friday.
Swapon highlighted that the Sanatan faith represents a thousand-year-old heritage and history bears witness to its long-standing continuity.
"Throughout human civilization, spiritual leaders across all faiths are striving to reach the Almighty. True believers respect and revere followers of other faiths because everyone is ultimately seeking the same Supreme Power, regardless of the ritual or path they follow," he added.
The minister urged everyone to stay vigilant against forces attempting to exploit religious sentiments for narrow political gains or societal division, both domestically and regionally.
"Staying firm in one's own faith while showing deep respect to other faiths to ensure peaceful coexistence is the true essence of a non-communal and inclusive society," Swapon stressed.
He further underscored that under the philosophy of Bangladeshi nationalism—as outlined by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman—no division based on religion, caste, language, or geography will be tolerated.
Inaugurating the event, Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) Administrator Abdus Salam stated that Bangladesh belongs equally to all communities.
"Those who seek to undermine communal harmony do not truly believe in Bangladesh's sovereignty. People of the Hindu faith fought alongside us during our Liberation War, and this nation was achieved through shared sacrifices. There is no scope for anyone to be considered a second-class citizen here; every citizen shares equal rights," Salam noted. Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad President Basudeb Dhar also spoke on the occasion as special guest.

item.title: Khalilur: Bangladesh to work closely for stronger Asean
item.description:
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman has reaffirmed Bangladesh’s commitment to working closely with Asean and its partners to strengthen regional cooperation in tackling emerging and transnational threats.
Addressing the commemorative ceremony marking the 50th anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia (TAC) in Manila, he stressed the need for practical and coordinated initiatives to bolster global resilience against pandemics, climate shocks, cyber incidents and supply chain disruptions, said a foreign ministry press release here on Friday.
Dr Khalilur said joint early-warning systems, shared risk assessments and regional crisis-response mechanisms could play an important role in strengthening collective preparedness and resilience against such challenges.
The foreign minister also outlined ways to address emerging threats posed by AI-enabled cybercrime as well as misinformation and disinformation spread through social media.
The TAC, signed five decades ago, establishes principles governing relations among states in the region, including mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity and non-interference in internal affairs.
Bangladesh acceded to the TAC in 2007, becoming one of the first South Asian countries to formalize a treaty-based commitment to Asean’s normative framework.
On the sidelines of the TAC anniversary events, Dr Khalilur Rahman also held separate bilateral meetings with the foreign ministers of Chile, the Netherlands and the Philippines, as well as Qatar’s state minister for Foreign Affairs.
The meetings covered a range of issues of mutual interest, including trade and investment, energy supply, water-resource management, legal migration and the circular economy.
Khalilur Rahman is currently visiting Manila to attend the 33rd Asean Regional Forum (ARF) Foreign Ministers’ Meeting and commemorative activities marking the 50th anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia.

item.title: 181 more dengue patients admitted to hospitals
item.description:
Around 181 dengue patients were admitted to various hospitals in the last 24 hours across the country. During the same period, there was no report of death from dengue, according to the Health Emergency Operation Center and Control Room of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Among the patients hospitalized with dengue, 57 are in the Dhaka Division, 25 in the Mymensingh Division, 71 in the Chittagong Division, 16 in the Khulna Division, two in the Rajshahi Division, seven in the Barisal Division and three in the Sylhet Division.
As of July 24, this year, a total of 12,201 people have been hospitalized with dengue.
A total of 39 people have died from dengue so far this year.
A total of 11,081 dengue patients have been discharged from hospitals.
From January 1 to December 31, 2025, a total of 102,861 people were infected with dengue, and a total of 413 people died from the disease.

item.title: Dhaka among 10 districts at risk as monsoon intensifies
item.description:
Bangladesh is bracing for another spell of stormy weather as an active southwest monsoon intensifies over the country, prompting the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) to issue warnings of thunderstorms, gusty winds and heavy rainfall across large parts of the country.
On Friday, the BMD forecast temporary gusty or squally winds of 45-60km/h, accompanied by rain or thunderstorms, over Dhaka, Faridpur, Khulna, Barisal, Patuakhali, Noakhali, Comilla, Chittagong, Cox's Bazar and Sylhet. Inland river ports in these districts have been advised to hoist Local Cautionary Signal No. 1.
The latest warning comes amid an increasingly active southwest monsoon, which has already triggered intermittent rain in several regions over the past week and is expected to continue influencing weather conditions in the coming days.
For the capital, the BMD forecasts partly cloudy to cloudy skies with rain or thundershowers throughout the day. South to southeasterly winds are expected to blow at 10-15km/h, while daytime temperatures are likely to remain nearly unchanged.
Official observations showed Dhaka recorded a temperature of 25.2°C at 6am on Friday, with 98% relative humidity, reflecting highly moisture-laden conditions. The city received 8mm of rainfall during the previous 24 hours, while Thursday's maximum temperature reached 31.2°C.
Meteorologists said the combination of high humidity and recurring rainfall is likely to keep conditions uncomfortable despite slightly lower temperatures.
According to the BMD's 24-hour nationwide forecast, most places in Dhaka, Khulna, Barisal and Chittagong divisions, along with many areas of Rajshahi, Rangpur, Mymensingh and Sylhet divisions, are likely to experience light to moderate rain or thundershowers accompanied by temporary gusty winds.
The department also warned of heavy to very heavy rainfall in Khulna, Barisal and Chittagong divisions, raising the risk of urban flooding, waterlogging and localized flash floods.
In the Chittagong Hill Tracts and adjoining hilly areas, prolonged rainfall may further increase the risk of landslides.
Meteorologists attribute the current weather pattern to an active southwest monsoon drawing abundant moisture from the Bay of Bengal. Combined with local atmospheric instability, the system is creating favourable conditions for widespread cloud formation, thunderstorms and intense rainfall.
Bangladesh typically experiences short-duration but high-intensity downpours during the monsoon season, particularly in coastal and southeastern districts.
Meteorologist Dr Md Bazlur Rashid said rainfall activity is expected to remain above normal over the next several days.
"The monsoon is currently active over Bangladesh, and this is likely to sustain widespread rain and thunderstorms across many parts of the country," he said.
He added: "Heavy to very heavy rainfall remains possible, particularly in the southern and coastal districts. People using waterways and those staying in open areas should closely follow official weather advisories."
Experts warned that the impacts of the current weather system extend beyond heavy rainfall.
High-intensity downpours could overwhelm urban drainage systems, worsening waterlogging in Dhaka, Chattogram and other major cities. Low-lying areas may experience temporary flooding, while prolonged rainfall in hilly regions could heighten the risk of landslides.
Lightning also remains one of Bangladesh's deadliest monsoon hazards. Authorities have advised people to avoid open fields, rivers, tall trees and electrical poles during thunderstorms, while operators of small boats have been urged to suspend operations when cautionary signals are in force.
With the monsoon expected to remain active through the weekend, the BMD said it will continue issuing updated forecasts and warnings as conditions evolve, urging residents to remain vigilant and follow official weather advisories.

item.title: Can Pakistan-administered Kashmir elections calm tensions?
item.description:
The first phase of local elections in Pakistan-administered Kashmir is scheduled for Monday, July 27, amid calls for a boycott from the recently outlawed Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (Jaac), a grassroots alliance of civil society groups.
The Jaac has been demanding the abolition of 12 seats in the regional assembly reserved for people displaced from India-administered Kashmir and living in Pakistan. It argues that only residents of Pakistan-administered Kashmir should be eligible to contest regional elections.
The dispute escalated after the Supreme Court of Pakistan-administered Kashmir ruled that the refugee seats are constitutionally protected and cannot be abolished without a constitutional amendment.
The regional government outlawed the Jaac in June under anti-terrorism laws, citing threats to public order, and detained dozens of its supporters.
The ban came amid rising tensions over the refugee seats and ahead of violent protests sparked by the group’s campaign to scrap them.
The unrest has left around 30 people dead since June, according to local estimates cited by Reuters news agency.
India and Pakistan both claim Kashmir in its entirety, but each country only controls a section of the territory, making the Muslim-majority region a longstanding flashpoint between the nuclear-armed neighbors since their independence from Britain in 1947.
Since early June, Pakistan-administered Kashmir — known locally as Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) — has witnessed weeks of protests and sit-ins. While the dispute over the refugee seats has become a major flashpoint, Jaac has also campaigned for broader economic and governance reforms.
Following the unrest, authorities split polling into three phases, with voting in Mirpur set for July 27 and elections in the protest-hit Poonch division postponed until August 10.
Voting in the regional capital Muzaffarabad has been delayed until August 2 over security concerns. The Jaac continues to stage a sit-in in Rawalakot, near the Line of Control with India.
As the region heads to the polls, a major question is whether the elections can restore public confidence or merely offer a temporary pause in public anger.
“We are just asking for fair representation, which is our right,” Ali Raza, a 22-year-old student protester in Rawalakot told DW. “The local people who live here should have the right to choose their representatives, not the refugees who settled here from India.”
“The election is a major opportunity for the people of AJK to choose their representatives,” said Shazia Marri, the central information secretary of the Pakistan People’s Party (PPP), which currently rules the region. “The people want their rights protected, their issues addressed, and a government that delivers on its promises.”
However, Jaac leaders argue that elections alone cannot resolve the issues that brought thousands of people onto the streets.
“Our movement is not replacing one government with another over time; we need our rights, but there are just political slogans in the campaigns,” one Jaac official told DW under condition of anonymity.
Imran Khan, a geopolitical expert and former director of the US Institute of Peace Pakistan, expects the movement to continue post-elections.
“While elections in AJK are important on their own merit and for the continuity of the political process, they will not address the political grievances and demands of the people who are supporting Jaac,” Khan told DW. “The protest is outside the assembly. They no longer trust those institutions fully.”
Analysts say the Jaac protests marked a significant shift in Pakistan-administered Kashmir’s politics by bringing together citizens across party lines around economic and governance issues rather than traditional political rivalries.
For analyst Khan, Jaac is a dominant political force to reckon with in quite significant parts of Pakistan-administered Kashmir.
“They have more street credibility than mainstream politicians and parties despite the allegations of foreign backing and funding. For now, they have disrupted the status quo politics in AJK,” Khan said, noting that the Pakistani establishment has the means and methods to break up such political movements.
Experts caution that rebuilding trust will require more than campaign promises.
“[The] next government in AJK will be very weak, as it will be sandwiched between pressure from both the Pakistani establishment that controls AJK through administrative and security framework and the sentiment on the street, which is very pro Jaac,” argued Khan.
He added that the next government would have “little credibility and limited room to govern unless it reaches an understanding with Jaac to ease political tensions.”
But politician Marri believes that trust is rebuilt by listening to people’s concerns, delivering practical solutions, and empowering elected institutions.
If key grievances remain unresolved, analysts warn that another wave of protests cannot be ruled out.
“It is too early to say that more waves of protests will be seen, but Jaac has the potential to become a lasting political force,” said Khan, who suggested the group risks being weakened by internal divisions and pressure from the establishment.
“For now, both sides are treading carefully, with Jaac relying on mass support and the establishment avoiding a full crackdown while buying time,” Khan added.
While the vote will determine who governs Pakistan-administered Kashmir, it is unlikely to resolve the broader constitutional dispute over Kashmir or eliminate long-standing frustrations with the region’s governance.
“Governments must listen to public concerns and address them through dialogue and effective governance. Stability comes from listening to people, respecting the law, and delivering results,” Marri added.
For Raza, the Gen Z protester, “The world has changed, and we have seen governments toppling through student protests in the neighboring countries; we won’t stop, and protests will continue until our rights have not been given to us.”

item.title: Klopp handed task of reviving Germany's football fortunes
item.description:
Jurgen Klopp was named as the new head coach of the German men's national football team on Friday, replacing Julian Nagelsmann who left after the team's disappointing World Cup.
"We're very happy to be able to present Jurgen Klopp today as the new coach," German Football Association (DFB) President Bernd Neuendorf told a press conference in Frankfurt.
Neuendorf said Klopp's contract would run until "summer 2030, so until the next World Cup in Morocco, Spain and Portugal," adding that the contract would begin on August 15.
Klopp, 59, had spoken publicly of his desire to take on the role after Nagelsmann left earlier in July.
Germany crashed out of this summer's World Cup after losing to Paraguay on penalties in the round of 32.
It was the third successive World Cup failure for the Germans since winning their fourth title in 2014.
Germany failed to make it past the group stage in both 2018 and 2022. They have won just one knockout match at the past five major tournaments, reaching the quarter-finals as hosts at Euro 2024.
Klopp had successful coaching tenures at German clubs Mainz -- where he was a player for more than a decade -- and Borussia Dortmund before turning round the fortunes of English giants Liverpool.

item.title: NCP demands arrest of Mohammed Shahabuddin following resignation as president
item.description:
The National Citizen Party (NCP) has demanded the arrest of Mohammed Shahabuddin following his resignation from the office of President.

The party voiced this demand during a press briefing held on Friday evening at its central office in Banglamotor, Dhaka.

NCP Member Secretary Akhter Hossen stated that Shahabuddin must be arrested immediately to ensure complete justice for the sacrifices of the martyrs of the 2024 mass uprising and to prevent the resurgence of an autocratic system.

He added that if the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) truly upholds the spirit of the July Mass Uprising, it should swiftly initiate legal action against the former president.

Akhter Hossen alleged that the resigned president was an accomplice to fascism who legitimised all forms of enforced disappearances and killings under former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.

Furthermore, during the 2024 uprising, when Sheikh Hasina perpetrated atrocities against students and the public, Shahabuddin tacitly endorsed her actions through his silence, the NCP senior leader added.

Akhter also remarked that although Shahabuddin stepped down citing ill health, he incorporated irrelevant historical narratives into his resignation letter in what was essentially an attempt to construct a 'safe exit' for himself.

Criticising the BNP in this context, member of parliament Akhter Hossen noted that the BNP had been informed long ago that Shahabuddin was unfit to hold the presidency. However, rather than impeaching him at the time, the BNP helped consolidate his position by involving him in various social and state functions.

The NCP leader asserted that while immunity had previously shielded Shahabuddin from legal proceedings due to his office, his resignation leaves him with no remaining legal protection.

Speaking at the briefing, NCP Senior Joint Convenor Ariful Islam Adeeb stated that the BNP wishes to install its own nominee in the presidency during the upcoming election period, which is why it initiated moves to remove the president five months after forming the government.

He added that the BNP has a history of placing pliable individuals in the presidency to secure electoral advantages, and that the current political maneuvering is merely a continuation of this longstanding strategy.

Also present at the briefing were NCP member of parliament Abdul Hannan Masud and NCP leader Monira Sharmin, among others.

item.title: Japan to test rare-earth mining 6 km underwater
item.description:
JAPAN-CHINA-MINING-OCEANS-CLIMATE

Japan said Friday it plans to conduct full-scale mining tests in February for rare earth minerals from a seabed near a remote Pacific island, after a mission successfully recovered samples from six kilometres below the waves.

Japan and the United States, as well as many other countries, are seeking to curb dependence on China for the valuable minerals used in an array of high-tech products from missiles to wind turbines.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said that the samples taken earlier this year by a deep-sea drilling ship from a depth of around 6,000 metres (about 20,000 feet) near Minami Torishima included traces of yttrium.

Yttrium "is globally scarce and is used in coating agents for semiconductor manufacturing equipment, catalysts for purifying harmful nitrogen oxides in exhaust gases, and in the semiconductor and automotive industries, making it an important rare earth for our country", Takaichi said on X.

"Based on this achievement, we plan to conduct a full-scale mining test in February next year."

Japan will "undertake efforts to strengthen the supply chain resilience, with the full involvement of both government and private sectors, so as not to overly depend on specific countries", Takaichi added.

The Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC) said separately that gadolinium and dysprosium, two other rare-earth elements, were also detected in the 50 tonnes of seabed material recovered.

In March, Takaichi said that she would discuss cooperation with the United States on mining around the coral atoll, which is some 2,000 kilometres (1,250 miles) from Tokyo and also known as Minamitorishima.

Previous studies have suggested that the surrounding seabed could contain millions of tonnes of rare earths which might ensure supplies of some minerals for many hundreds of years.

Environmental campaigners warn deep-sea mining threatens marine ecosystems.

China accounts for almost two-thirds of rare earth mining production and 92 percent of global refined output, according to the International Energy Agency.

A spat with Beijing sparked by comments by Takaichi about Taiwan in November has seen China heavily restrict supplies to Japan.

Officials said in March that they also planned to conduct a preliminary survey on Minami Torishima, uninhabited by civilians and off-limits to tourists, as a possible site for nuclear waste.

item.title: Bomb recovered beneath Motijheel metro station
item.description:
Police have recovered an improvised explosive device (IED) concealed inside an umbrella beneath the Motijheel metro rail station in the capital.

The device was subsequently rendered safe by the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) bomb disposal unit.

According to DMP sources, the device was found on the road beneath the Motijheel metro station at around 7:30 pm on Friday. The suspicious package, hidden inside an umbrella, caused panic among passers-by.

On information, police members quickly cordoned off the area before the DMP’s bomb disposal and disposal team arrived at the spot and successfully neutralised the device. Traffic on the affected road was temporarily suspended during the operation.

Niaz Mehdi, Additional Deputy Commissioner of the DMP’s Media and Public Relations Division, told Prothom Alo that the recovered device was an improvised explosive device (IED).

He said it had been safely removed and rendered inoperative. Police and other law enforcement agencies are now working to identify those responsible for placing the device inside the umbrella.

Witnesses said a loud explosion was heard while the bomb disposal team was carrying out the controlled detonation to neutralise the device.

Contacted for comment, MRT Police Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Siddiqi Tanzilur Rahman told Prothom Alo that he was occupied preparing an official report and was therefore unable to speak about the incident.

However, an officer on duty at the MRT Police Control Room confirmed that the device had been recovered from the roadside beneath the metro station. As a result, traffic movement on the adjacent road was temporarily halted, although Metro Rail services continued to operate normally throughout the incident.
